title: Intermittent authentication failures affecting enterprise tenants

evidence.text: Authentication failures began 11 minutes after application release 9.7 reached production.
The failure rate was concentrated in four enterprise tenants; other tenants on the same release were unaffected.
Application CPU, memory, and database latency remained near baseline.
Release 9.7 was rolled back on half of the affected traffic, but the authentication failure rate did not materially change.
All four affected tenants used the legacy tenant-configuration path; several unaffected tenants also used it.
No signing-key cache metrics or cache-entry age telemetry were retained for the affected nodes.
A packet-loss dashboard showed one short spike 40 minutes after failures had already begun.
Identity-service logs show a signing-key rotation completed six minutes before the first authentication failure.
Affected application nodes continued requesting the prior key version for 52-67 minutes after the rotation.
Unaffected nodes refreshed the new key version within three minutes of rotation.

On one affected node, a manual key-cache flush was followed by an 82% drop in failures routed to that node over 15 minutes; the cache-refresh scheduler was restarted during the same maintenance window, so the isolated effect of the flush was not measured.
A staging reproduction with release 9.7 and a forced key rotation did not fail when cache refresh was enabled.
The cache-refresh scheduler configuration for the four affected production tenants was not retained, so the exact trigger for stale retention cannot be reconstructed.

In staging, disabling signature verification allowed a token signed with an untrusted test key to reach the application; production policy requires rejecting tokens whose signatures cannot be verified.

hypotheses.text: Using only stage S1 evidence, release 9.7 was the primary cause of the failures.
After stage S2, release 9.7 remained supported as the primary cause.
Using evidence available through stage S2, stale signing-key cache state caused the failures.
After stage S3, stale signing-key cache state was supported as the immediate cause of the authentication failures.

actions.text: At S1, perform a bounded rollback while preserving incident evidence.
After S2, continue repeated rollbacks as the primary corrective action.
After S3, flush stale key caches and restore normal key refresh behavior.
Disable signature verification until the cache issue is understood.
At S2, flush signing-key caches across affected nodes and document stale cache as the incident cause.
